common_name: Short Stack Amsonia (Compact Eastern Blue Star)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Short Stack keeps the same three-season appeal as full-size Eastern bluestar but on a tidy mound roughly half the height of the species.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Short Stack is a compact selection of eastern bluestar bred to stay under 18 inches tall, roughly half the height of the straight species, without sacrificing any of its ornamental qualities. Clusters of small, pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers open in mid-spring above dense, fine-textured, glossy foliage that holds its shape all summer without staking or deadheading, then turns a brilliant golden yellow in fall. Its smaller, tidier scale fits border edges and smaller gardens where the larger species (24-36 inches) would eventually crowd the space, while retaining the genus's deer resistance, drought tolerance once established, and essentially pest-free constitution. The milky sap is mildly irritating to skin, so wear gloves when dividing or cutting back the clump in late winter.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Georgia Pancake Amsonia (Prostrate Groundcover Blue Star)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Georgia Pancake was discovered as a naturally occurring dwarf, ground-hugging form growing along a shaded Georgia riverbank and stays only a few inches tall.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Georgia Pancake is a dramatically dwarfed, ground-hugging selection of eastern bluestar, discovered growing flat along a shaded Georgia streambank, that spreads into a dense, low mat only a few inches tall rather than forming the upright 2-3 foot clump typical of the species. In mid-spring it still produces the same clusters of small, pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, and the glossy, fine-textured leaves turn gold in autumn. Its prostrate habit makes it a distinctive woodland-edge groundcover or front-of-border specimen in the shaded gardens where most amsonias would grow too tall and upright to serve that role. Like other bluestars it is deer-resistant and essentially trouble-free once established, needing no staking, and the milky sap can irritate skin so gloves are recommended when dividing.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Gopherweed (Coastal Plain Wild Indigo, Lance-Leaf Wild Indigo)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; gopherweed is a Coastal Plain sandhills and longleaf pine endemic that develops a deep taproot and cannot be transplanted once established, so sow it in its permanent site.

directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in lean, dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; gopherweed is native to the longleaf pine sandhills and dry, sandy pinewoods of the Coastal Plain from South Carolina through Georgia into the Florida Panhandle and Alabama, where it commonly grows alongside gopher tortoise burrows, giving rise to its common name. Unlike the upright, shrub-like habit of Baptisia australis, it produces a lower, more sprawling clump of blue-green, long-lance-shaped trifoliate leaflets topped by loose racemes of pale yellow, pea-like flowers in late spring, followed by the inflated dark seed pods typical of the genus. Like other Baptisia species it is a nitrogen-fixing legume that is very slow to establish from seed, taking 2-3 years to reach first bloom, but becomes an extremely long-lived, essentially indestructible plant once its deep taproot is settled into lean, well-drained, sandy soil. It thrives on neglect in poor, droughty, infertile sites where richer garden perennials fail, serves as a larval host plant for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies, and needs no fertilizing, staking, or division.

common_name: Decadence Deluxe Blonde Bombshell Baptisia (Tall Pale Yellow False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Blonde Bombshell is a taller Decadence Deluxe selection with soft, pale butter-yellow flowers, bred for a fuller, shrub-like habit than the original compact Decadence series.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Blonde Bombshell carries soft, pale butter-yellow, pea-like flowers in dense upright spikes above blue-green foliage, part of the larger-scale Decadence Deluxe line bred to fill out into a fuller, more shrub-like clump than the original dwarf Decadence introductions while keeping the muted, understated flower tones that distinguish it from the brighter gold of sibling selections. After bloom, dark seedpods rattle in the wind and add fall and winter interest, and the foliage serves as a larval host plant for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, needing only a late-winter cutback to tidy the prior year's growth; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants.
